messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samir has spent fifty-four years of his life on rooftops, a trade he learned from his father in another country and a life he built with his own hands in America. At seventy-eight, he still possessed a tradesman’s wiry strength, but for the last six months, that strength had felt like a lie. The precipitating event was a job he took last spring, re-shingling a commercial building that shared a property line with a small public park. It was a sunny Tuesday, and the sounds of children playing on the swings drifted up to him as he worked. The crash was deafening, a screech of metal followed by a concussive boom that shook the roof beneath his feet. A tanker truck carrying industrial solvents had overturned on the adjacent road. A thick, acrid cloud, the colour of pale mustard, began to billow out, rolling low and fast across the grass of the park. Panic erupted below. He remembers the screams, the sight of parents snatching their children and running, but the memory itself is fractured. When he tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events, to build a story from it, the pieces won't connect. It's like a film strip that was burned in the projector, leaving only disconnected, scorched frames.

What he cannot control, however, are the fragments that force their way into his mind. He will be sitting at the dinner table with his wife, Layla, and suddenly he is back on that roof, the chemical stench catching in his throat, the high-pitched wail of a child piercing the air. More unsettling are the times the feeling comes without any picture at all. He can be watching a nature documentary, a perfectly peaceful scene, when a wave of pure, unattached terror washes over him. It’s a cold dread that starts in his stomach and seizes his entire body, the same helpless horror he felt that day, but with no image to anchor it. He is left gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs, with no explanation for Layla, who sees only a man suddenly terrified of nothing.

Since the accident, Samir’s world has shrunk. He used to enjoy the evening news, a ritual he and Layla had shared for forty years. Now, the television remains off. Any mention of chemical spills or industrial accidents, even in other states, can trigger the suffocating feeling. He saw one of the other men from the work crew at the grocery store a month ago and immediately abandoned his cart, hurrying out a side door before he could be seen. The most painful change has been with his grandchildren. When his daughter brings them to visit, the sound of their laughter, once his greatest joy, now feels like a prelude to disaster. He finds himself retreating to the garage, feigning work on a tool, unable to be in the same room. He has come to believe that something terrible is always on the verge of happening, that he is no longer capable of keeping anyone safe.

This constant state of alert has ravaged his body. He cannot relax, not even in his favourite armchair with the window open to the garden. His muscles are perpetually coiled, ready for a threat he cannot name. When Layla comes up behind him and places a hand on his shoulder, he flinches so violently he nearly knocks her over, his mind screaming *danger* before he can even register it is her. Sleep offers no escape. He lies awake for hours, his mind racing, and when exhaustion finally claims him, he wakes an hour or two later, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding a frantic rhythm against the mattress. The fatigue has made his work precarious. On a roof, balance and focus are everything, and he has neither. He feels brittle, one misstep away from a fall. It was after he dropped a hammer, startled by a car backfiring on the street below, that he knew he could no longer continue working. The loss of his trade, his identity, was a profound blow. He finally sought help after his seven-year-old granddaughter asked Layla why Grandpa didn't want to play with her anymore. The question, relayed to him gently by his wife, broke through the wall of his avoidance. He is here not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is terrified of becoming a ghost in his own family, and he desperately wants to be able to hear a child laugh without feeling the world is about to end.
